title: Codex of the Third Beis HaMikdash reconstruction
aboutThisFile: A browsable reference for everything in this build. One entry per thing, each with the source it rests on and an honest label for how firm that source is.

The three labels are the point of the file. 'certain' means the sources agree or one is decisive and nothing cited disputes it. 'disputed' means they disagree, and the entry names who holds what. 'authored' means nobody said it - the project chose it because a model has to put something somewhere.
Where a receipt in SourceAssets records what was actually built and to what size, the receipt is cited by path, and where the built number differs from the sourced number the entry says both.

The primary text is the author's Hebrew book 'Lishchno Tidreshu'. Only its Third Temple layer - the Ketz HaYamin (קץ הימין) sections - is treated as a claim about this building; its historical layers describe the Mishkan and the first two Temples and are marked as such.
None of this is rabbinically approved and none of it is practical guidance.

confidenceLabels.certain: The sources agree, or one source is decisive and no cited authority disputes it.
confidenceLabels.disputed: The sources disagree. The entry names who holds what.
confidenceLabels.authored: Nobody said this. The project chose it because a model has to put something somewhere.

sourceLayers.book-ketz-hayamin: Lishchno Tidreshu, the Ketz HaYamin (קץ הימין) layer: the author's Third Temple summary per verse. Primary for this project.
sourceLayers.book-biur-chai: Lishchno Tidreshu, the Ba'or Chai (באור חי) layer: sources and reasoning.
sourceLayers.book-hashlamas-sheres: Lishchno Tidreshu, the Hashlamas Sheres (השלמת שרת) layer: completions from Torah, Middos and Rambam, often describing the Mishkan or the earlier Temples.
sourceLayers.halachic: Mishnah, Talmud, Rambam. Evidence for the institution described, not automatic proof of every detail of the future House.
sourceLayers.receipt: A JSON or Markdown record under SourceAssets of what this build actually made and where.

cautions: The Ketz HaYamin paragraph for a verse is reprinted on every page of that verse in the book. Repetition is not independent confirmation.
Diagram 22:28 on p. 257 is the Third Temple. Diagram 22:27 on the same page, with ten menorot and ten tables, is the First Temple. Do not read the second as this building.
Do not name a court in this model after a Second Temple court merely because it looks similar.

localization.hebrewPolicy: Hebrew NAMES are filled where the term is a standard Hebrew name. Hebrew PROSE is empty and marked hebrewProse:"not-authored" - an English fallback the reader can correct beats a Hebrew paragraph he has to unpick.

name.en: The amah, and how long it is

summary.en: Everything here is measured in amot, and the physical length of an amah is not settled. This model is baked at a round 50 cm per amah, which is a modelling decision and not a ruling. The common opinions run from about 48 cm to about 58 cm, so the same 3000-amah square is 1440 m a side under one and 1740 m under another - without a single vertex moving. One object is measured differently on purpose: the golden altar uses the five-tefach amah of Eruvin 4a, 41.67 cm.

name.en: The size of the precinct: 3000 amot or 500?

summary.en:
This is the single largest open question in the reconstruction, and it changes the scale of everything.

The reading this model is built on: Yechezkel 42:15-20 measures the sacred precinct with a reed, five hundred by five hundred. A reed is six amot (Yechezkel 40:5, 'a reed of six amot, an amah and a tefach'). Five hundred reeds is therefore 3000 amot a side - about a kilometre and a half at any of the common amot - and Rashi reads it that way. The book adopts it as certain, notes the Kalir piyut on the figure, and points out that this makes the future Mount thirty-six times the area of the Second Temple's.

The other reading: Mishnah Middot 2:1 gives the Har HaBayit of the Second Temple as 500 amot square. Read Yechezkel's five hundred as amot rather than reeds and the future precinct is the same size as the old one. The research assembled for this project does not find the book arguing that case for the Third Temple - it uses the 500 amot as the Second Temple comparison figure that the thirty-six-times ratio is computed against, and takes Middot 2:1 for the shape and proportions rather than the magnitude. Anyone who holds the 500-amah reading is entitled to it; this entry is stating what the source pile in this project actually contains, not settling it.

A third position, and it is the author's own: an inner soreg ring of 500 amot square inside the 3000, with the cheil inside that. The research marks this explicitly as 'the author's forced reading', starred for study, and it is the only place the 500-amah figure survives into the Third Temple in his account.

What is actually built: the enclosure in this map is the 3000-amah square, 150,000 cm a side, with its wall faces at X -33100 to 116900 and Y -33150 to 116850. The Future Mount platform underneath it is only about 377 m square, so the ring is far larger than the terrain it stands on. That mismatch is a recorded gap, not a claim.

name.en: The House does not stand in the middle

summary.en: The Sanctuary sits toward the north-west of the precinct, not at its centre. Open ground is largest to the south, then east, then north, and least to the west, and the city lies on the slope to the south. That asymmetry is why the enclosure in this model is centred at [41900, 41850] rather than on the Temple, and why the clearances come out as 500 amot west, 501 north, 2176 east and 2175 south.

name.en: The terumah, the portion around the precinct

summary.en: Yechezkel 45:1 and 48:8-20 describe a consecrated portion of land 25,000 on a side around the precinct. Whether those 25,000 are amot or reeds is itself disputed, which is a six-fold difference. This model draws the ring in amot and labels it rather than deciding.

name.en: The wall of the Mount and its five gates

summary.en: A wall six amot thick and six amot high runs round all four sides of the precinct, dividing what is holy from what is not. Five gates pierce it: two on the south, one each on the east, north and west. Each opening is ten amot wide and fifty high, with doors. The extra ten amot of wall carried above the opening - making sixty in all - is the author's, marked for study.

summary.en: A wooden lattice ten tefachim high running round the court, well inside the precinct wall. It is low enough to step over, which is the point: it marks a line rather than blocking one. It is built here at 83.33 cm, at a radius of about 10,250 cm from the Temple centre.

Inside the soreg comes the cheil, and what the cheil is depends on whom you follow. The Rambam, the Meiri and Mishkenei Elyon read it as a wall ten amot high with ten amot of open ground inside it, and that is what is built here. The Bartenura and the Tosafos Yom Tov read the soreg itself as the cheil's wall, leaving only the open strip. The one-amah thickness given to the wall in this model is the book author's own, offered for study.

name.en: How the whole complex steps upward

summary.en: Nothing here is level. The mountain slopes down on all four sides; the outer court gate floors sit below the inner court; the Court of Israel sits two and a half amot below the priests' court; the House stands six amot above that; and the Even HaShtiya rises three fingerbreadths above the House's floor. The step counts are firm - twelve steps at the east outer gate, seven at the north and south, eight at every inner gate, twelve to the Ulam. The slopes and the exact western levels are the author's.

There is no west gate anywhere in this plan. It is a hundred amot from any gate to the gate facing it across the court.

summary.en: Each outer gate is a block twenty-five amot wide: five of wall, two and a half, the ten-amah opening, two and a half, five. Six cells line its passage, three a side. In front of it a vestibule projects ten amot into the court, its interior thirteen by eight and fifty high, flanked by two round pillars two amot square and sixty high with palm capitals. Twelve steps climb to the east gate, seven to the north and south, because the ground is higher there.

name.en: The cells in the gate passage

summary.en: Six chambers, three on each side of the passage, each six amot square inside with five-amah walls, projecting eleven amot outward on the Mount side. They are chain-linked one to the next and can be entered only from the passage itself. The five-amah cell walls rising to fifty and a ceiling spanning the passage - so that the vestibule, the passage and the gate are covered continuously - is the book author's proposal.

The windows are built the wrong way round on purpose: narrow on the inside and widening as they go out, the opposite of a window meant to gather light. They carry no glass and are never closed. Where they are and how many is another matter - the counts in this model are the book author's, and Rashi's gloss about them being sealed from within is treated in the book as a corrupt reading.

name.en: The thirty chambers on the gallery

summary.en: Thirty chambers stand on a gallery whose floor is fifty amot up - the same height as the gate openings. Ten on the east, ten on the south, ten on the north, five to each side of every gate, and none at all on the west. That much is Rashi and Mishkenei Elyon. Their size, their height and the suggestion that they are where women stood are the book author's.

summary.en: Four unroofed courts, forty by thirty amot, one in each corner of the outer court, where the lesser holy offerings were cooked. No piers and no gallery run over them.

summary.en: Everyone entering the Mount turned right and circled, leaving by the left. A mourner, or someone under a ban, went the other way round, so that whoever met him coming the wrong way knew and could ask what had happened to him.

The outer east gate is the gate of entry all year round, except at the three festivals, when the crowd enters by the north and leaves by the south, or the reverse. The inner east gate is different: it opens on Shabbos and on Rosh Chodesh and on no other day. On an ordinary weekday the way into the inner court was through the lower chambers, which have a door into the Court of Israel. This model has no lower chambers, so the tour walks up a gate that would be shut.

The inner gates are the outer gates turned back to front. Eight steps instead of twelve or seven, and the vestibule projecting outward into the great court with the cells behind it, so a person climbing goes vestibule, then steps over the eleven amot of cells, then gate. There are three of them and no more.

name.en: The names of the three inner gates

summary.en: That there are three inner gates and not the seven or thirteen of the Second Temple is settled. What they are called is not. The book maps the north to the gate of the offering, because kodshei kodashim are slaughtered on the north side, and the south to the water gate, because the water of Yechezkel 47:1-2 flows out from the Kodesh HaKodashim through the southern inner gate; he floats a gate of the firstborn as well. The research records this mapping explicitly as the author's, not the navi's.

summary.en: Recesses twenty-five amot by five are set into the thickness of the inner court wall, one on each side of each inner gate, leaving half an amah of wall on each face. That they are twenty-five by five is Rashi. That there are six of them is the author's reasoning from there being three gates, and their twenty-five-amah height is his too. They are not in this model at all - a recorded gap.

name.en: The slaughter tables and the rinsing chamber

summary.en: Eight tables belong at the north inner gate: four inside its vestibule, two east and two west, and four in the cell passage at the gate's own floor level. The vestibule, although it stands in the outer court, carries inner-court sanctity. At the gate's west shoulder is a closed chamber with four stone tables an amah and a half square and an amah high, and eight low cedar posts carrying iron hooks a tefach long in three rows. In this build the eight tables are not at the gate at all: they sit clustered inside the court at X -1188 to -663, Y -2088 to -1812. That is a recorded gap, not a reading.

name.en: There is no Women's Court here

summary.en: Every plan of the Second Temple has an Ezras Nashim east of the Israelite Court. This plan does not, and neither does this model: the research assembled for this project contains no Third Temple row describing one, and the word appears nowhere in the build's receipts. The nearest thing in the book is a suggestion that women may have used the thirty gallery chambers of the outer court, and the research marks that as the author's, after the Second Temple's balcony. Saying 'we found nothing' is a result. It is not the same as saying there was none.

name.en: Why the House stands thirteen amot further west

summary.en: The altar's site is fixed and cannot move. So when the distance from altar to porch grows from the Second Temple's twenty-two amot to thirty-four, and the partition of the Kodesh HaKodashim grows from one amah to two, the whole House shifts west by thirteen amot. The Zohar's answer to the obvious worry - that the Aron would then no longer sit on the Even HaShtiya - is that the stone fills the whole chamber.

summary.en: The Levites sang at the wine libation of the daily offering, morning and afternoon, standing on the duchan and facing east. Their instruments were kept in the chamber at the east shoulder of the north inner gate.

Thirty-two amot square, in the exact centre of the inner court, thirty-four amot from the porch. That much is Yechezkel 40:47 as Rashi and Mishkenei Elyon read it, and everything else in the plan is measured from it because its site is fixed forever.

What this project does NOT have from the sources is the altar's own build-up. The volume of the book read here covers Yechezkel 40 to 42 and defers the altar's height, yesod, sovev and horns to a note on chapter 43 in a second part that is not in the export. So the tiers, the ramp's width and slope and the horn heights in this model come from the architecture manifest and not from a text, and they are labelled authored here for that reason. The Gemara's rule is that the Torah's altar measures are not indispensable - it may be made larger, never smaller than Moshe's.

name.en: What licenses a vessel Yechezkel never mentions

summary.en: Yechezkel names one piece of furniture in the House - the table of 41:22 - and no others. The menorah, the golden altar, the Aron and its keruvim, the kiyor and its base are all absent from his account. Rashi, the Radak, the Tosafos Yom Tov and Mishkenei Elyon take the Torah's furniture as continuing unless the navi cancels it, and the book records that as certain. That principle is what allows this reconstruction to contain anything at all beyond the walls; it is worth knowing it is a principle and not a verse.

sources: Rashi, Radak and Tosafos Yom Tov as gathered in Mishkenei Elyon 177

name.en: The stepped lintel over the porch is Second Temple

summary.en: Five stepped olive-wood beams above the porch entrance, each projecting an amah further at each side, are Middot 3:7 describing the Second Temple. They are not described for this House, and the book says so. The layered stone lintel and cornice in this model are that Second Temple styling carried over by mistake - a recorded gap, not a reading.

Forty amot long, twenty wide, with walls six amot thick on all four sides. Its doorway is ten amot wide and fifty high - twenty in the Second Temple - with a square frame: threshold, straight lintel, two jambs, and nothing round or five-sided about it.

Two pairs of leaves, each leaf five amot wide and fifty high. The outer pair sits an amah in from the jamb and folds back onto the five amot of wall thickness, the extra amah being the door's own thickness; the inner pair stands at the Sanctuary face and folds onto the five-amah shoulders inside. That is the Tanna Kamma's arrangement, followed by the Rambam and the Ramchal, and it is the one the book builds. Rashi also carries R' Yehudah's version of the folding. The western pair was opened first each morning, then the eastern, and they were locked each evening by way of the small northern door. In this model the doors are four flat slabs protruding into the Sanctuary - a recorded gap.

name.en: Why there is cedar under the gold

summary.en: Gold cannot be laid directly on stone. So the walls, jambs, doors and ceiling of the Sanctuary and the Kodesh HaKodashim are panelled floor to ceiling in thin cedar boards, carved, and the gold is beaten into the carving so the forms stay visible, fixed with gold nails. Only the window openings are left bare. In this Temple, unlike the last, the wall behind the doors is lined too. No wood is left exposed anywhere in the House or the courts. That the floor is also carved boards under gold is the author's.

sources: Melachim I 6:32 with Rashi, Radak and Malbim

name.en: The keruvim and palms on the walls

summary.en: Every wall of the Sanctuary and the Kodesh HaKodashim carries an alternating carving: keruv, palm, keruv, palm, floor to ceiling, on the jambs and the doors and above the entrance. Each keruv shows two faces and only faces - not a body: a young lion's face on the keruv's right, turned to the palm on that side, and a man's face on its left, turned to the palm on that side. The two faces and the alternation are in the navi and Rashi. Which face goes on which side is Mishkenei Elyon, who reads the lion as the right and so as chesed. The six wings the book gives them are his own speculation. None of this has been modelled: the walls in this build carry gold and a palm-only study panel, and the keruvim have never been made. It is the largest recorded gap in the reconstruction.

name.en: The House, a hundred amot every way

summary.en: The House measures a hundred amot long, a hundred wide and a hundred high. The length adds up exactly: porch wall 5, porch 11, Sanctuary wall 6, Sanctuary 40, partition 2, Kodesh HaKodashim 20, west wall 6, west chamber 4, chamber foundation 6. The width is the porch's twenty with forty-three of wall on each flank and the two knife chambers. The height of a hundred is certain; the layers the author breaks it into - eighty-five of interior, six of otem, five of ceiling, three of parapet, one of spikes - are his. For contrast the First Temple was a hundred and twenty and the Second a hundred, and the book's reading of why is kabbalistic rather than architectural.

summary.en:
Every lamp that had gone out had its wick and leftover oil taken away and the lamp cleaned; a new wick and a fresh half-log of oil went in, and it was kindled. The Rambam says that kindling is what the word hatavah means - and the Moznaim note on that passage records that other authorities take hatavah as the cleaning alone. This build depicts the Rambam.

The kohen came in carrying a golden vessel, put the spent wicks and oil into it, kindled five lamps, left the vessel on the second of the three steps and went out; then came back, kindled the remaining two, took the vessel, prostrated himself and left.

Who does it: ordinarily an ordinary kohen, chosen by the lottery of Temidin uMusafin chapter 4. The Kohen Gadol may perform any service he wishes on any day without entering the lottery, and Mishnah Yoma 1:2 names the lamps among the services he performs during his seven days of sequestering - so depicting him doing it is legitimate.

name.en: Two citations this project got wrong and fixed

summary.en:
Both corrections were found and recorded by the agent that built the Kohen Gadol's service, and they are carried here so they are not quietly re-broken.

First: the ruling that the Kohen Gadol may perform any service he wishes without entering the lottery is Rambam, Klei HaMikdash 5:12, not 5:11. 5:11 is a different halachah - it describes him entering the Sanctuary to prostrate, supported by three attendants, one holding the jewels of the choshen so it does not shift from the ephod. That halachah is independently useful: it is direct evidence that he walks into the Sanctuary in the golden garments.

Second: that the lamps face the centre is Rambam, Beis HaBechirah 3:8, not 3:12. Beis HaBechirah 3:12 is the Shulchan. Temidin uMusafin 3:12 is the definition of hatavah - both 3:12s are real and each is cited for what it actually says.

Nothing in any source fixes any of them. They are pacing choices, and the whole loop runs 290.5 seconds because those numbers were picked, not because the service took that long.

summary.en:
Incense is offered on the golden altar morning and afternoon. The morning offering falls between the blood service of the daily offering and the bringing up of its limbs; the afternoon one between the limbs and the libations - these are relative positions in the service, not clock times. While the incense burns everyone withdraws from the Sanctuary and from the space between the porch and the outer altar, until the kohen who offered it comes out.

Where in the lamp sequence it falls is not settled. Abaye's order of service puts it after the second group of lamps; the Rambam's own note at Temidin uMusafin 3:17 sets the re-entry after the limbs were brought up. This build follows Abaye, and the passage in Yoma 33a was not independently verified in the pass that recorded it. Treat the relative position as unsettled.

Nothing about the incense is modelled: no particles, no emitter, no smoke.

name.en: The smoke, and what nobody knows about it

summary.en:
Yoma 53a describes the smoke rising like a staff to the ceiling and then spreading down the walls until the chamber is full, and distinguishes putting the incense on the fire inside from carrying a cloud in ready-made. Yoma 38a records the Avtinas family's column against the Alexandrians' dispersing smoke, and a descendant who could recognise the herb and would not name it.

What none of that establishes is a plant. The research for this project states flatly that no secure botanical identification of maaleh ashan has been made, and that no modern species, chemical mechanism or recovered sample may be labelled as the authentic ingredient. Colour, opacity, rise speed, thickness, particle size, smell and how long it lingers are all artistic choices.

summary.en:
A wooden box two and a half amot by one and a half by one and a half, with an inner gold box a tefach smaller and an outer a tefach larger, a gold crown around it, four rings at the top corners and gold-covered poles permanently in them. Inside it the Luchos, the broken Luchos and a Sefer Torah. On it the kaporet, a gold slab a tefach thick - and that thickness is a rabbinic derivation, not a measurement in the verse. Beside it Aharon's staff, the jar of manna and the flask of anointing oil.

All of that was missing from the Second Temple, along with the fire, the Shechinah and the Urim v'Tumim. Where the Aron stands is disputed: the Rambam puts it on a stone in the western part of the chamber, the Tosafos Yom Tov and the Tanchuma in the middle. And Yirmiyahu 3:16-17, with Rashi, speaks of an era when it is not spoken of again - a passage that must be acknowledged, and which should not be flattened either into a prohibition on depicting it or out of existence.

In this build there is an Aron study at [-6200, 0, 925] in sixteen parts. The project's own audit found no finished Aron mesh in the architecture manifests and recorded the Kodesh floor package as a source-derived chamber envelope, not an established Aron location.

An ordinary kohen may enter the Sanctuary every day, for service. The Kohen Gadol enters the Kodesh HaKodashim once a year, on Yom Kippur, and nobody else ever does. All kohanim are warned not to be in the Sanctuary or the chamber beyond it when they are not in the middle of a service; this model's depicted service has no idle wandering for that reason.

One caution: the Rambam extends the verse's 'within the curtain' to the whole House, and the Kessef Mishneh questions that reading. Where the tour walks past those lines it says so.

summary.en: The camp of Israel is the whole city up to the Mount, including where the kohanim and Levites live around it. The camp of the Levites runs from the Mount's gate to the vestibules of the three inner gates - the outer court, the eleven amot behind the House, the lower chambers. The camp of the Shechinah begins at those vestibules and goes inward. A non-Jew and anyone bearing corpse impurity stop at the cheil; someone who has immersed but whose day has not ended stops at the outer court.

name.en: Immersion, and three things it is not

summary.en:
Three separate ideas get run together and the sources keep them apart.

Corpse impurity is not cured by a bath at all: it needs the purification water and the third and seventh days and then immersion and the ending of the day. A bath is not a universal reset.

Exclusion is graded by zone. The Rambam distinguishes what bars a person from the Mount, from the cheil, from the Women's Court and from the Israelite Court, and corpse impurity, someone who has immersed but whose day has not ended, and someone still owing an offering are not interchangeable.

Immersion before service is its own requirement, described in Yoma for someone already pure. It must never be implemented as clearing an existing state of corpse impurity. Sanctifying hands and feet at the laver is a further and separate prerequisite that no immersion replaces.

No mikveh has been built in this model and the research gives no Third Temple location for one; where the book places mikvaot in the lower chambers, that placement is his own.

sources: Lishchno Tidreshu p. 324 (the mikvaot placements - the author's)

summary.en:
An ordinary kohen wears four garments: tunic, breeches, head covering and sash. The Kohen Gadol wears eight, and his Yom Kippur linen set - tunic, breeches, turban and sash - is a service-specific outfit for part of that day, not a replacement for everything he wears through it.

Several points are open and must not be quietly decided. Whether the Kohen Gadol's sash is the same as an ordinary kohen's is disputed between the Rambam and others. The pomegranates on the hem of the robe are drawn both open-mouthed and closed. The Temple Institute holds two reconstructions of the ephod, one after the Rambam and one after Rashi, and they differ in how it sits. The modern identification of several of the breastplate stones is not settled. Even whether the words on the head plate run on one line or two is disputed.

There is no Kohen Gadol garment asset in this project at all. The figure in the service sequence wears a pilgrim material and says so.

name.en: The water that comes out from under the threshold

summary.en: Yechezkel 47:1-2 has water coming out from under the threshold of the House eastward and passing out by the southern gate. The book takes the southern inner gate as its way out, and that is the source point this scene would use. It is not modelled.

Three things are worth knowing before trusting any entry here.

First, the labels mean what they say. 'Certain' means the sources read for this project agree; it does not mean the matter is beyond argument, only that no cited authority in this pile disputes it. 'Disputed' names the disagreement. 'Authored' means the project made it up, and every 'authored' label in this file is a place where the model is more confident-looking than the evidence.

Second, a source about the Mishkan or the first two Temples is evidence for the institution, not automatic proof of a detail of the future House. The book itself works in three layers and only its Ketz HaYamin layer is a claim about this building.

Third, 'unknown' is a result. It is not the same as 'permitted', and it is not an invitation to fill the gap. Things this project looked for and did not find are recorded as not found - the altar's own dimensions, the kiyor's size, any Women's Court, the order of the seven lamps, the identity of the smoke-raising herb, and a rabbinic approval of any of it.
